summary: Defines a framework for authentication and authorization in Internet of Things settings, based on OAuth 2.0 and CoAP. It turns a widely used authorization approach into a form suitable for small devices, reusing existing specifications where possible and adding extensions and profiles for IoT use cases.

plainLanguage.summary: A small gadget gets a permission slip from a trusted office before a door opens, in a way small devices can handle.

questions: what is a proof of possession token
subtitle: OAuth 2.0 reshaped for tiny devices: CoAP, CBOR and proof-of-possession tokens instead of bearer tokens over HTTPS.

tldr.problem: Many Internet of Things devices have little power, memory and processing speed, and cannot always use full OAuth 2.0 with HTTP, JSON and TLS to decide who may access them.
tldr.mechanism: ACE-OAuth keeps the OAuth 2.0 roles (client, authorization server, resource server) but adds CoAP and CBOR encodings, proof-of-possession access tokens bound to a key, an authz-info endpoint on the resource server, and profiles that pick concrete security protocols.
tldr.outcome: A constrained device can be authorized with compact messages and tokens it can store and check itself. Concrete deployments are defined by separate profiles such as RFC 9202 and RFC 9203.

today: RFC 9200 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2022. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines the framework only; concrete deployments use profiles such as RFC 9202 (DTLS) and RFC 9203 (OSCORE), and the extra key parameters are in RFC 9201.

sections.title: Why OAuth Needs Adapting for IoT
sections.content:
Authorization means granting an entity approval to access a resource. In the model used here, a client (C) wants a resource hosted on a device, the resource server (RS), and one or more authorization servers (AS) mediate that access.

Many IoT devices are constrained in processing capability, memory and energy. The RFC lists common limits in Appendix A: low-power radios, slow CPUs, small amounts of memory, limited user interfaces and unreliable connectivity. Sending and receiving messages can cost roughly ten times more energy than AES, so fewer and smaller messages matter.

The design aims to cover a continuous range of devices and networks, from battery-powered to mains-powered, rather than one fixed deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: Tiny gadgets have small batteries and little memory, like a toy with a very small backpack. The normal way of asking permission is too heavy to carry, so this makes a lighter version.

sections.title: The Building Blocks
sections.content:
ACE-OAuth is assembled from existing pieces. OAuth 2.0 is the base framework. CoAP is a web transfer protocol similar to HTTP that typically runs over UDP. CBOR is a compact binary encoding used where JSON is too large. COSE provides object-level security, and the default token format is the CBOR Web Token (CWT).

CoAP use is RECOMMENDED in constrained environments, and CBOR is RECOMMENDED even when CoAP is not used. Other transports such as HTTP/2, MQTT, Bluetooth Low Energy and QUIC are not ruled out. If a future profile uses a protocol without RESTful verbs, it MUST say how the messages are carried.

The RFC deliberately does not mandate one security protocol. DTLS and OSCORE are named as examples, and any protocol meeting the requirements in the security section can be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of inventing everything new, the designers picked small, light versions of parts that already existed, like choosing travel-size bottles for a trip.

sections.title: The Basic Protocol Flow
sections.content:
The client asks the AS's token endpoint for an access token (step A) and gets back the token plus Access Information, such as the key to use and the profile the RS supports (B). It then presents the token to the RS (C) and gets the protected resource (F). If the RS wants fresh information, it can ask the AS's introspection endpoint about the token (D, E). That step is optional and can be skipped when the token is self-contained.

The framework assumes the client and the RS were each registered with the AS beforehand, by means outside this document, such as factory provisioning or a commissioning tool. The keying material for the client-to-RS link is set up dynamically by the protocol.

Two OAuth grant types cover most scenarios: the authorization code grant for phone or tablet apps that reach IoT devices, and the client credentials grant for constrained clients whose access rights were prearranged. Authorization endpoint use is out of scope because the main use case is machine-to-machine.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask a trusted office for a pass, the office gives you the pass, and you show it at the door. Sometimes the door guard phones the office to double-check.

sections.title: Discovering the AS and Getting Hints
sections.content:
A client must find the AS in charge of an RS and must validate that this AS may issue tokens for that RS. It can send an Unauthorized Resource Request to the RS. The RS treats a request as unauthorized if it came over an unsecured channel, if the RS has no valid token for the sender, or if the token does not cover the action. It denies the request and SHOULD include AS Request Creation Hints.

The hints are a CBOR or JSON map with an optional AS element (an absolute URI), plus optional audience, kid, scope and cnonce elements. The CBOR keys are 1 for AS, 2 for kid, 5 for audience, 9 for scope and 39 for cnonce.

The client-nonce (cnonce) helps an RS whose clock is not synchronized with the AS. The RS stores it, the client copies it into its token request, the AS puts it in the token, and the RS discards any token whose cnonce is missing or not fresh. The hints arrive over an unprotected channel, so the client must not blindly trust them.
sections.plainLanguage: If you try a door without a pass, the guard points you to the right office and may hand you a secret word to repeat there, so they know your pass is brand new.

sections.title: Token and Introspection Endpoints
sections.content:
The client sends a POST to the token endpoint, by default named /token. Compared with plain OAuth 2.0, grant_type becomes OPTIONAL (default client_credentials), scope may be a byte string, and audience can request a token for a specific RS. Over CoAP the parameters are sent as a CBOR map in the POST payload instead of URI query parameters, with Content-Format application/ace+cbor (ID 19).

By default the AS generates a symmetric proof-of-possession key. To use an asymmetric key or reuse an existing one, the client uses the req_cnf parameter defined in RFC 9201. A successful reply is the equivalent of CoAP 2.01 (Created). The response adds ace_profile and makes token_type optional, with PoP assumed by default.

Errors use code 4.00 (Bad Request), except invalid_client, which MAY use 4.01. Two new errors exist: unsupported_pop_key and incompatible_ace_profiles.

The introspection endpoint, by default /introspect, is optional. The requesting entity POSTs a map with a token entry. The response follows RFC 7662 with additions: ace_profile, cnonce, cti and exi. An inactive token is not an error. The AS answers with active set to false.
sections.plainLanguage: The forms are shrunk to short numbered codes so the messages fit in a small envelope. A form with a number 24 for the name box takes less space than the long word.

sections.title: Presenting and Checking Access Tokens
sections.content:
The RS exposes an authz-info endpoint, by default /authz-info, where the client POSTs the access token. The RS MUST verify the token before storing it and, if valid, answers with the equivalent of 2.01 (Created). It MUST be prepared to store at least one token, which differs from OAuth 2.0 where the token is usually sent with each request. Storing only one token per proof-of-possession key is RECOMMENDED, because it keeps the RS simple.

Verification first checks the token's security wrapper and that the AS had the right to issue it. Then the RS checks claims in a fixed order: iss, exp, aud and scope, with different error codes for each failure. Using CWT is RECOMMENDED, and self-contained tokens MUST be integrity protected.

When the client later makes a request, the RS answers 4.01 (Unauthorized) if no proof of possession was done or no valid token exists, 4.03 (Forbidden) if the token does not cover the resource, and 4.05 (Method Not Allowed) if it does not cover the action.
sections.plainLanguage: You hand your pass to the guard, who checks the stamp, the date and the room name before putting it in a drawer. Later, the guard checks that you really are the pass's owner.

sections.title: Token and Key Expiration
sections.content:
An RS can check expiry in three ways. It can compare exp and nbf claims against a clock synchronized with the AS. It can ask the AS through introspection, which needs a reliable connection. Or it can use the new exi (expires in) claim, which gives a lifetime in seconds counted from the moment the RS first receives the token. This works only for self-contained tokens.

To avoid unbounded memory growth when tracking expired exi tokens, the AS MUST put a cti claim in the token, built from the RS identifier plus a sequence number. The RS stores the highest expired sequence number and treats lower ones as expired. Drawbacks noted in the security section are that a malicious client may hold back tokens to prolong their lifespan, and that an RS which loses state may lose its counters.

Clients cannot see inside the token, so they must assume the keys are valid only as long as the token is. They learn that either from a default validity time or from the expires_in parameter. A client that cannot learn the expiry MUST NOT use the token.
sections.plainLanguage: Passes need an end date. If the guard has no clock, the pass says how many minutes it lasts from when the guard first sees it.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Communication between client and AS, between RS and AS, and between client and RS after the token is delivered MUST be encrypted, integrity protected and replay protected, with responses bound to requests. Profiles must name the protocol that provides this. Initial client-to-RS contact cannot be fully secured, so DTLS without client authentication is RECOMMENDED if both sides support it.

Tokens must be integrity protected. A symmetric key placed in a token MUST be encrypted so only the RS can read it. Tokens for several recipients need an asymmetric signature, and the same shared secret MUST NOT be used as a proof-of-possession key with multiple RSs. Revocation beyond client-initiated revocation is left to future work.

Leaked proof-of-possession keys let an adversary impersonate the client, and physical extraction is a real risk for constrained devices. Secret keys used for authentication MUST NOT be shared between more than two parties.

On privacy, the AS sits in a central position and can learn what clients want to do. Unencrypted tokens and unprotected hints can reveal audience, scope or the RS's relationships. If the RS uses introspection, it MUST NOT allow access based on a token when it cannot reach the endpoint, and rate limiting of the authz-info endpoint is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep your secret key safe, because anyone with it can pretend to be you. Also, a pass that shows too much about you can give away private things, so passes should say as little as they can.

items.text: The base authorization framework with client, AS and RS.

items.title: CoAP
items.text: A web transfer protocol like HTTP, typically over UDP.

items.title: CBOR
items.text: A compact binary encoding for small code and message size.

items.title: COSE
items.text: Object-level security, used to protect tokens.

items.title: CWT
items.text: The default CBOR Web Token format for access tokens.

items.desc: A token exists but does not authorize access to the requested resource.

items.desc: A token exists but does not cover the requested action on the resource.
